chapter_theme: In the envoy sarukkam the young women of the city plague the men with the arts of desire, then turn to serve the Vidyadhara guest, and at the king's bidding Vijayan and Tivittan ride out in procession while the women swoon on the terraces.

cast.role: the young women of the city who plague the men and then serve the guest
the young men who suffer and speak to the women
the Vidyadhara guest, taken to be the envoy of the sarukkam
the king who bids the princes ride out

455.reading: The poet says that in the smoke of incense bees take the women's bright eyes for blue lilies and their hands for kanthal flowers and swarm at them, and the women are sorely pained.
455.nuance: The grammar of lines 1-2 is compressed; the women are taken as the sufferers, but the verse could also be read of the men pained at the sight.
455.event: Bees mistake the women's eyes and hands for flowers and the women are pained by them.

456.reading: The poet pairs the women's looks with things that delight: hair with bees, hands with sugar cane, sweet songs with lute strings, the nectar of the lips with the bud-like teeth.

457.reading: As men in fragrant garlands bow their hearts to the women, the women's wide eyes, struck by desire, dry within and wilt, and they bow back as if before a goddess.
457.nuance: The pairing of bowing in line 4 is hard to place; it may be the men who bow to the women as to a goddess.
457.event: The men bow to the women and the women bow back, both pained by desire.

458.reading: The poet says the men, saying the oiled hair of the women would burn them like fire and their long dark eyes can kill, worship them and break down, begging to be spared if the women should scorch them with their breasts.
458.event: The men worship the women and collapse, saying their hair burns and their eyes kill.

459.reading: The poet says these women were reared as the living pattern of the lore of love, with trailing hair and the forms of garlanded creepers, and shown as proof of the Kama manual.
459.nuance: The first line names the lore and the arts of learning as a good path; line 4 makes the women its example.

460.reading: The poet says the women, reared with swelling breasts, bloom like cool flowers for those they love, melt like fruit sweet as sea-ambrosia for them, and turn in anger like Kama's five arrows.

461.reading: The poet says their sulks call for union and their unions breed sulks, so that these young women with red lips go about holding Kama's five arrows.
461.nuance: The play of sulk and union is the stock pairing of love poetry; here it is cast as the work of Kama's arrows.

462.reading: The men, seeing the bodiless Kama only through these women, say they will somehow bear him, and cry out in wonder at what sin the Creator committed in making them, since here they have found the root of his birth.
462.nuance: The speaker of lines 3-4 is not named; they are read as the men of the scene, and the Creator is only exclaimed against, not argued with.

claims.claim: women's beauty is where desire is seen to take birth, and so the Creator's making of them is blamed

463.reading: The poet says that as the fire of desire blazed within them, fine lines of hair rose from the girdle across the belly, like smoke-lines, toward the breasts.
463.nuance: The body is read as the women's; the 'smoke' is the line of fine hair, which the verse makes the sign of fire within.

464.reading: The men ask the women why their faces darken, and say that if they were gone to the forest to bear small austerities then to be angry at others would be understood, but they linger in sandal paste.
464.nuance: The verse is a question put to the women; its first lines are hard to construe and the sense of vanavar or ascetic guardians is read loosely.

465.reading: The men say that when they see Kama's long bow, with arrows, bent on the faces of these women, it is hard to say why they should still hold on to their sweet lives.
465.nuance: The bow is read as the women's brows set on their faces; the poet leaves the image unexplained.

466.reading: After the men's cry the women go off like creepers drawn on cloth to the Kalpaka grove, hurrying to tell Kama of their victory over the army of lovers.
466.event: The women leave the men in pain and go to the Kalpaka grove to report their conquest to Kama.

467.reading: The poet lists what the women carry: one a cloth, one a jewelled vessel, the attendants strings of gems, others garlands of cool gems in their hands.
467.event: Women carry cloths, jewel vessels and garlands.

468.reading: The poet lists what the women bear: caskets of colour, flower-garlands, perfumed powder and trays of gems, with all that was wished, and the young women go in step.
468.event: The young women carry colours, garlands and powders in jewelled caskets.

469.reading: As the women with golden vessels of omen go to the man, followed by others, the faultless Vidyadhara in his bright garland decides that this must be heaven.
469.nuance: That the guest is the Vidyadhara envoy of the sarukkam's title is read from the sarukkam, not stated in the verse.
469.event: The women go with auspicious vessels to the Vidyadhara, who judges the place to be heaven.

470.reading: The Vidyadhara sits and thinks these are what those who reach heaven gain; the young women set aside their sidelong looks and little smiles and devote themselves to the guest-duty owed to the man in the room.
470.nuance: The women keep their looks for the lovers of verse 466 and turn them off for the guest; the verse makes hospitality a duty that cuts across the arts of desire.
470.event: The women put away their glances and smiles and serve the guest.

471.reading: The women bathe him, anoint him with sandal paste, garland him and feed him a meal of six tastes, so that he shines as one of the gods.
471.event: The women bathe, anoint, garland and feed the guest.

472.reading: Women named Tilakai, Kalyanikai, Senai and Kamalamalai, who are like moving flower creepers, attend him, and the old-famed lord of the sky is glad.
472.nuance: The four names are clear from the Tamil but the word ambarasaran at the end is split in the text and read as the guest.
472.event: Four named women attend the guest, who is pleased.

473.reading: At the king's bidding Vijayan, called the conch-coloured one, mounts the great trunked elephant together with Tivittan, ready for battle.
473.nuance: Whether the verse sends the princes to war or to a procession is not stated; the sarukkam's theme of sending an envoy points to a march out.
473.event: At the king's order Vijayan and Tivittan mount a war elephant.

474.reading: The poet says the elder brother mounts the elephant with a golden brow-band and a gem on its neck, and sits there like a white moon rising with a dark cloud above the red-gold mountain.
474.nuance: Line 1 reads as a headline for the verse, not as a line of the metre, and is damaged.
474.event: Vijayan and Tivittan mount the elephant.

475.reading: The poet lists the crowd that gathers: musical instruments, elephants, chariots with warriors, people, fly-whisks, white banners, kings in sweat and the women with flowing hair.
475.nuance: The verse is a single run of nouns with no verb; it describes the procession.

476.reading: Singers, bowers, those who bless with long life and dancers join the throng, and women in the mansions faint, their garlands slipping and their breast-ornaments falling.
476.event: The women on the mansion terraces faint as the princes pass.

477.reading: The women with cloud-like hair, faces like the full moon, earrings and golden ear-leaves lean out, with garlands swaying, and then are hidden in the mansion windows.
477.event: The women look out from the mansion windows and withdraw.

478.reading: The women on the upper storeys, hair clustered with bees and garlands slipping, look like dancing peacocks.

links.note: Verse 458 has men grant that the women's long dark eyes kill and bow to them; Naladiyar 44 refuses to call eyes spears or carp, since he has seen the eye is a scooped-out palm fruit.
links.teaches: The Soolamani gives the lover's image of the lethal eye a scene of surrender, and the Naladiyar answers with a renunciant who would not give way, so a reader sees the image only works on one who agrees to be struck.

gains.a: A refusal of the image of the killing eye, which the verse alone only enjoys.
gains.b: A scene in which men yield to the very image the renunciant's resolve is set against.

links.note: Kural 1085 asks whether the young woman's look is Death, an eye or a doe; verse 458 says the women's long dark eyes are skilled at killing.
links.teaches: The eye as Death is a shared trope of the lover's tradition, which the epic makes the plea of many men at once.

gains.a: The Kural's own line that the look is Death, which sets this plea in a known convention.
gains.b: A crowd of men instead of one man, the Kural's one lover made general.

links.note: Verse 462 has men blame the Creator for making women, whose beauty they take as the cause of desire; Tirumanthiram 204 turns the same beauty into an etti fruit that looks good and poisons, and tells the heart to hold back.
links.teaches: The men's wonder at the Creator's sin shows desire as a thing done to them, and Tirumular sets it as a choice of the heart, which marks where the epic stops short of the Saiva remedy.

gains.a: A remedy for the cry of the men, who only blame the Creator.
gains.b: A scene of men who feel the beauty the verse warns against, and who blame another for it.

links.note: Verse 463 puts a fire of desire within the women that sends up lines like smoke; Naladiyar 89 says desire burns the mind itself and is more to be feared than arrow, fire or sun.
links.teaches: The epic shows the fire of desire as marks on the body, and the Naladiyar says what the fire burns, the mind, so each supplies what the other lacks.

gains.a: A statement that this fire burns the mind and is worse than outer fires.
gains.b: A body in which the fire shows as smoke-lines of fine hair.

links.note: Verse 83 says the fire of desire burns women within and none bears it more heavily than the shame-bound; in verse 465 the men voice it aloud to the women.
links.teaches: The epic first shows desire borne in silence by women and then spoken freely by men, so the burden is set unequally by who may say it.

links.note: Verse 53 says that in this king's days nothing but Kama's arrows mingled in the land and no killing force troubled it; verse 466 has the women report to Kama their victory over an army of lovers.
links.teaches: The earlier verse treats Kama's war as the only gentle one, and here it has victims and a victor, which shows the gentle war is still a war.

links.note: Verse 50 says the golden city seems an Indra's heaven come down to earth; verse 469 has a Vidyadhara, who knows the sky, judge that this is heaven.
links.teaches: The poet's praise of the city as heaven is confirmed by a sky-dweller who can compare, so the boast is turned into an outsider's verdict.

links.note: Kural 84 says a glad face towards good guests draws the goddess of wealth; verse 471 shows the host women doing every service to the guest for the Vidyadhara.
links.teaches: The Kural's rule is given a court in which welcome is a trained skill and not a feeling, and the Kural shows what the women's service is for.

gains.a: A rule that the welcome depends on the host's face, which the women who set aside their looks only half meet.
gains.b: A setting in which the guest-duty is done by those whose art is desire.

links.note: Verse 81 says the women swoon with fear that the dark-gemmed prince, who came in a dream, will take their lives; verse 476 has the women faint on the terraces as the princes pass.
links.teaches: The dream-fear of the women becomes a public swoon, so the epic shows the prince's coming as the fulfilment of the fear.

source_issues: Verse 474 line 1 reads as a rubric, not a line of the metre, and its words are damaged.
Verse 463 line 1 reads வளைர்ந்த for வளர்ந்த.
Verse 472 line 4 splits அம்பரசரன் across the word break.
Verse 469 line 4 shows a doubled line break in துகளில் விஞ்சையன்.
Verse 462 ends with a full stop and is the only verse of the run to do so.
